author: Jacob Steinberg
description:
The former midfielder with impressive managerial promotion record began with a thrilling comeback in draw at Cardiff

Three days in and Scott Parker has already lost his voice. West Ham’s head coach arrived on Tuesday, watched his side fight back from 3-0 down to draw with Cardiff on Wednesday and was struggling to make himself heard when he met the media on Thursday afternoon.

“It’s like in the summer holidays,” Parker said. “You put the flip-flops on for five weeks, then you come back home and you get your shoes on. You’re in a minute, you’ve got a blister on the back of your heel. It’s the same with a throat. I’ve not shouted for a little while. All of a sudden there’s shouting and it’s a bit croaky.”
title: Scott Parker’s dramatic West Ham return leaves him struggling for words

author: Sid Lowe
description:
Only 3,587 people live in his family’s village but the streets of Navahermosa were fuller yet quieter to mourn the Tenerife striker at his funeral

The narrow streets of Navahermosa in La Mancha were fuller than they have ever been on Thursday afternoon and quieter too. Silence accompanied the funeral cortege as its made way from the funeral home to the parish church of San Miguel Arcángel carrying Jesús de Miguel Alameda, “Demi”, the Tenerife striker who died after an on-field collision with the Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono three days earlier. Only 3,587 people live in his family’s village but now they were joined by the game he loved. “We wanted to be close to his parents, his wife and daughter. In moments of pain, football comes together more than ever,” said Luis de la Fuente.

The Spain manager did not say much else; there was not much else he could
title: ‘In moments of pain, football comes together’: Spain says goodbye to Jesús de Miguel

author: Michael Hogan
description:
Heston Blumenthal is a third wheel as the pair reveal all about their culinary stardom and infamous beef. Expect endless juicy gossip, from pan-throwing to gatecrashing weddings … and mid-service kitchen sex

Never mind the scallops, here’s the Chef Pistols. Rise of the Rockstar Chef portrays the fine-dining dons of the 90s and 00s in the manner of a band biopic. In place of musical differences is a stolen reservations book and an argument about red mullet that reduced Gordon Ramsay to tears. How’s that for a kitchen nightmare?

As Ramsay, Marco Pierre White and Heston Blumenthal look back at their storied careers, it’s a culinary willy-waving contest. “We were bigger and better than the Beatles,” brags White. “And we fed more people than they did.” It’s hard to argue with the latter claim, unless you count Linda McCartney’s veggie sausages.

Continue reading...
title: Rise of the Rockstar Chef review – Gordon Ramsay and Marco Pierre White serve up the most sizzling TV of the year

author: Matt Hughes and Ali Martin
description:
• Division One side have offered Anderson a contract

  • Nottinghamshire also monitoring seamer’s situation

Jimmy Anderson has opened talks over signing for Surrey next season with the club growing in confidence that England’s leading wicket-taker will agree to join them for what would be a remarkable swansong.

The 44-year-old has been inundated with expressions of interest since being released by Lancashire last month after 25 years at Old Trafford, with Surrey understood to have made a firm move by offering him a contract.

Continue reading...
title: Jimmy Anderson in talks with Surrey to continue county career after Lancashire exit

author: Betsy Reed
description:
A note from our US editor: A reckoning is coming, but make no mistake: Trump is still president – we’ll need a free press in 2027 as much as we did in darker days. Please help today if you are able

  • Betsy Reed is US editor of the Guardian

Over the past two years, millions of people all over the world have watched Donald Trump’s destructive reign unfold with one question in their minds: Is there no check on his power?

This week, voters deciding who controls Congress responded in a thunderous voice: there must be a check on the president’s power. From Texas to Ohio to South Carolina, Americans surged to the polls to register their opposition to Donald Trump – and to show their support for the kind of leaders who will look out for the interests of everyday people rather than those of a corrupt ruling elite. And now many people are looking at politics with a new and
title: US midterm voters responded in a thunderous voice. This is just the beginning | Betsy Reed

author: Kim Darroch
description:
Power is draining away at home, but the US president will see a chance to make his mark through foreign policy

  • Kim Darroch was Britain’s ambassador to the US between January 2016 and December 2019

Election nights are party time in Washington. The bars and restaurants fill up and the city rocks. For diplomats, it’s an opportunity – but it’s also a long night, as you trek across the party scene in search of insight and illumination. Invariably, it has its moments. I recall being at the Washington Post party on the night of the presidential election on 8 November 2016. Washington is an overwhelmingly Democrat city and the atmosphere was raucously optimistic, reflecting Hillary Clinton’s small but consistent lead in the polls. As the first results came in a shocked hush fell across the room. People gathered in small, murmuring groups. Within 30 minutes, half
title: I know the dangers a wounded Trump presents – this is how the UK should deal with him now | Kim Darroch

author: Editorial
description:
Patterns of drug supply and use are changing and the government’s five-year-old drug strategy must evolve too

A slight drop in the number of drug deaths over a year in England and Wales is the first such news since 2012. Over the past decade, the grim trajectory has been upward; the annual figure of 5,519 has more than doubled since the 1990s. Given this trend, any fall is a relief. But the spike in deaths linked to cocaine, which has overtaken heroin for the first time, as well as evidence uncovered by the Guardian of a link with domestic violence, points to the need for a drugs policy that takes account of changing usage.

Nearly six in 10 drug tests on people arrested on suspicion of domestic abuse were positive for cocaine in the year to June, w
title: The Guardian view on cocaine and domestic abuse: new links between drugs and crime need investigating | Editorial

description:
Kirill Dimitrov, envoy to Russian president Vladimir Putin, delivered a gift to Melania Trump at the White House on Thursday to thank her for brokering a ceasefire between Ukraine and Russian forces in Oleshky, Ukraine. During the same event, Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets gifted the first lady with the Order of Princess Olga, 1st Degree award.

Continue reading...
title: Putin envoy thanks Melania Trump for brokering ceasefire – video

author: John Crace
description:
New recruit Angus MacIntyre bears an unfortunate resemblance to little-missed ex-Tory minister Chris Grayling

You can make a good case for Nigel Farage having been one of the most consequential British politicians of the 21st century. Without him there would have been no Brexit. And yet it is now beginning to look as if his time has come and gone.

The narcissistic qualities that have served him so well now threaten to finish him off. His skin is becoming thinner by the day. All that’s left is reflexive lashing out. A raging against the dying of the light. You’d need to have a heart of stone not to laugh.

Continue reading...
title: Failing Grayling double reports for duty as Reform’s armed forces spokesperson | John Crace

author: Emine Sinmaz
description:
Level of interest in comedian’s case resulted in examination of affairs inside and outside the courtroom

Russell Brand’s trial at Southwark crown court, which ended with him being found guilty of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others, was one of the most obsessively watched criminal cases in recent history. As well as Brand’s own conduct, the case became an examination of his victims’ evidence, the legal strategy his team used to defend him, and the culture within which he committed his crimes.
title: Flashbulbs, lies and victim blaming: how Russell Brand’s trial unfolded

author: Jakub Krupa
description:
With flights disrupted, how concerned should you be about your travel plans?

  • Europe live – latest updates

More than 30 planes have been subjected to security alerts or diversions this week, with at least 25 more bomb threats on Thursday disrupting civil aviation across Europe.

What do we know so far, and how concerned should you be about your travel plans?

Continue reading...
title: Why have more than 30 European flights been hit by bomb threats this week?

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Readers respond to the recommendation by an independent commission that the profession be regulated

The independent commission established by the professional bodies that represent counsellors and psychotherapists in the UK makes a case for statutory regulation that is long overdue (Report, 2 November). Ella Janneh, who won damages in a civil case against her therapist, is right that most people assume the safeguards already exist, and the commission is right to say that they do not. What happened to her shows what that mistaken assumption can cost.

I write as the chairperson of the Irish Association of Humanistic and Integrative Psychotherapy and as a psychotherapist for more than 20 years. I tra
title: Regulation of counsellors and psychotherapists would protect patients | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Academics question the purpose of the carer’s allowance and say we can learn from the Scottish government’s reform process

Your editorial (27 October) is right: serious issues with the Department for Work and Pensions’ administration of carer’s allowance run far deeper than inadequate IT systems. Well-documented systemic failures and flawed design have caused preventable financial and emotional harm. While the abolition of the punitive “cliff edge” is welcome, a taper cannot be the extent of the government’s commitment to carers.

The unacceptably long timeline for implementation prolongs the injustice. How will the government protect carers who are at risk of incurring overpayments debt in the period until 2030-31? Following the revelation that the DWP has completed
title: Carers deserve a new, fairer social contract | Letter

author: Guardian Staff
description:
They help volunteers to develop skills, make friends and find employment, says Antony David Davies

Your article on the declining profitability of charity shops struck a chord with me (UK charity shop profits plummet amid shift in secondhand clothes market, 31 October). Having spent many years managing charity shops and community reuse projects, I feel that something important is being overlooked.

Charity shops were never just about making money. They provided affordable goods for people who needed them and, equally importantly, opportunities to gain confidence, develop skills, make friends and sometimes find their way back into employment. For some, volunteering is their first step back into society after a difficult period in their lives.
title: Charity shops have value in the community | Letter

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Bread runs in Oxford | Animal licences | Tomatoes in November | Cereal killers | Listening to Trump

I agree with Rev Nicholas Bradbury of Oxford (Letters, 2 November) about the sad disappearance of healthy wholemeal bread. I find sourdough indigestible and expensive. Fortunately, Nash’s bakery in Blackbird Leys, Oxford, sells excellent wholemeal bread. A group of us take it in turns to do the weekly “bread run” by bike or bus from Osney Island and Marston – much to the amusement of the friendly shop staff.
Clare Addison
Oxford

• Your correspondent’s plea for dog licences (Letters, 1 November) reminded me of my primary school in the 1950s. In preparation for the 11-plus exam, one of the “intelligence test” questi
title: Give us this day our wholemeal bread | Brief letters

author: Charlie Allenby
description:
What do you get the man who doesn’t seem to want anything? From fiery condiments to chef’s knives, slippers to portable speakers, these ideas are sure to hit the spot

• The best Christmas gifts for mums in 2026

Gifts for dads, grandads and other father figures can often feel like a shot in the dark. What do you get for someone who doesn’t seem to want anything, or who already has it all?

Shared experiences or promises of peace and quiet are popular options, but they are tricky to wrap. Which is where my recommendations come in.

Continue reading...
title: The best Christmas gifts in the UK for dads, grandads, uncles and friends – tested for 2026

author: Presented by Pippa Crerar and Kiran Stacey; music by Axel Kacoutié; executive producer Maz Ebtehaj
description:
As Donald Trump licks his wounds from a bruising set of midterm election results, the UK will look nervously to what he might do on the international stage in order to cement his legacy. Plus, Pippa and Kiran discuss what lessons Labour can take from the Democrats, and ask if they in turn can learn from Andy Burnham’s rise to power

Continue reading...
title: What can Andy Burnham learn from the ‘blue wave’ in the US? – podcast

author: Amy Fleming
description:
Huge, ecstatic canvases are just one of the vocations of the musician who joined the art rockers in 2024. As her show Hotwire My Heart opens, she talks terror, awe and teabags

Emma Richardson loves to eavesdrop when people look at her paintings and talk about what they see in them. “They turn into these Rorschach inkblot tests,” she grins. Looking at her works, you do stand back in awe wondering. Is that a nebula, a god or a fleshy, baroque orgy? An explosion, an implosion or an orgasm? Richardson implies all of these and more, her paintbrush chasing in vivid oils the hedonism, desire and breadth of human experience.

This fascination with the transcendent has in part been informed by her other life as a musician, formerly in the garage-rock trio Band of Skulls and currently playing bass and singing in Pixies.

Continue reading...
title: Is that an explosion, an implosion or an orgasm? Pixies bass-player Emma Richardson’s realm-leaping life in painting

author: Rebecca Shaw
description:
Trump is still president, and we don’t know where things will go from here – but sometimes it just feels good to see some terrible people have a terrible time

The last couple of days have been very bad for Donald Trump. Of course, in Trump’s usual style, he is denying that the Republican loss at the midterms has anything to do with him – but we all know it does. While I fear the Democrats will not use this decisive moment to exercise some ambition and take meaningful action, the goings-on of the last couple of days have been undeniably fun to watch.

Seeing so many conservatives lose in such a spectacular way has blessed millions across the globe with powerful schadenfreude. It is a much needed moment of relief, an experience of positivity to rejuvenate our ailing nervous systems (or whatever biology does). Sometimes you just
title: Seeing Trump and his acolytes lose so spectacularly is powerful schadenfreude for millions across the globe

author: As told to Rich Pelley
description:
The actor answers your questions about trapeze lessons, Bond villain ambitions and Michael Caine’s top tips

You looked as if you had such a good time on Celebrity Traitors last year – you had them hanging on your every word. What was it like? Who have you kept in touch with? breezehillpete
They absolutely didn’t hang on my every word. I’m fascinated to watch it now, because at a distance, I can see how people follow each other. That herd mentality is very evident at the round table, but I always went in a different direction and people didn’t follow me. Then, of course, I accused Alan [Carr] at the end: “I think you are one, aren’t you?”, so I had to go the next day. I didn’t quite know what I was letting myself in for, but I had a great time.

Kate [Garraway] and I had to go on that Uncloaked thing after. She turned to me and she said: “Oh, but Celia, we’re now all one big happy family, aren’t we?” I said: “Well, frankly,
title: ‘George Lucas told me off for wearing lipstick’: Celia Imrie on Traitors, Star Wars and treating the lens like a lover

author: Mina Holland
description:
High-protein, alcohol-free beer? The end times are here. But surely some of these ubiquitous protein drinks are drinkable … aren’t they?

As someone who is not unlikely to be tasting wine at 10am on a Tuesday, I am clearly not best placed to offer health advice. But, for the purposes of this column, I can tell you that every day most adults need 0.75g protein for every kilogram of body weight. This is achievable through a wholefood diet (nuts, pulses, eggs), although some people, namely athletes, supplement that with protein powders to support really quite profound levels of exertion.

In case it has escaped your notice, protein is a big deal right now, and products reformulated with added protein are popping up all over the place; it’s a phenomenon linked to the rising popularity of weight-loss drugs. Trouble is, they’re marketed at everyone, and it could be very easy to feel that you’re cheating yourself if you don’t opt for these enhanced versions of ordinary
title: No great shakes: the quest for palatable high-protein drinks

author: Peter Bradshaw
description:
Gong simmers with rage, loneliness and humiliation as the ‘fourth mistress’ navigating the intimate political savagery of her husband’s compound in Zhang Yimou’s 1991 thriller

Revisiting Zhang Yimou’s grippingly addictive psychological drama from 1991, adapted from a novella by Su Tong, is a reminder of what a great impact this movie made on western audiences. They responded to its arguably westernised tale of a young woman’s desperate loneliness in a sinister environment that resembles something by Charlotte Brontë or Daphne du Maurier. Like Jung Chang’s memoir Wild Swans from the same year, Raise the Red Lantern opened our eyes to 20th-century China’s secret theatre of cruelty and misogyny; elaborate domestic rituals of submission and servitude c
title: Raise the Red Lantern review – Gong Li gives a decade-defining performance in an addictively ruthless masterpiece

author: Jessica Glenza
description:
The wins for Democrats come after years of cuts and upheaval to US health and science infrastructure

A political organizations behind a wave of Democratic doctors and scientists winning elections up and down the ballot is calling the stunning rebuke of Trumpism the “Stem swing” and “revenge of the nerds”.

The wins come after years of cuts and upheaval to US health and science infrastructure, as Democrats spent big on health-related ads and as voters rejected the Make America Healthy Again (Maha) movement.

Continue reading...
title: ‘Revenge of the nerds’: US midterms deliver a win for science – and a rebuke of Maha

author: Guardian sport and agencies
description:
• 22-year-old also has eight blocks in Spurs win

  • Frenchman scores decisive free-throw in victory

Victor Wembanyama set a career high with 24 rebounds, then sank the winning free throw with 24.2 seconds left to ⁠cap his career-best 52-point performance as the San Antonio Spurs outlasted the Dallas Mavericks 112-111 for their sixth straight victory.

The Spurs home crowd hailed Wembanyama with MVP chants on Wednesday, and he also excelled on defense. The Frenchman blocked eight shots, three which of came in a span of just 13 seconds in the second quarter.

Continue reading...
title: ‘He’s basically Wilt’: Wembanyama downs Mavericks with 52-point, 24-rebound classic

author: Guardian community team
description:
Is there anything you would like to ask the former Ipswich, Rangers and England defender?

Terry Butcher has lived a full life in football. He won the Uefa Cup while playing for Ipswich under Bobby Robson; he was an England regular throughout the 1980s, winning 77 caps and playing at three World Cups; he captained Rangers in their late 1980s heyday; and he had a varied coaching career that started at Coventry City and took him to Australia, China and the Philippines. He’s also Pat Nevin’s cousin, one of only two England players born in Singapore, and, of course, a heroic figure when in a blood-soaked shirt.

Not many people in the game have experienced as much as Butcher. So, if you have a question, drop it in the form below and we will put it to him.
title: Post your questions for Terry Butcher

author: Guardian community team
description:
We’d like to hear from passengers and airline staff caught up in the disruption caused by a series of bomb threats to commercial flights

Multiple flights across Europe have been diverted or forced to make emergency landings following a series of bomb threats this week, prompting security checks and widespread disruption.

Are you on one of the affected flights or has your journey disrupted? What happened, and how did you feel? What information were you given by the airline or authorities, and how was the situation handled?

Continue reading...
title: Tell us: have you been affected by the bomb threats to flights in Europe?

author: Hosted by Carter Sherman and Kai Wright with Blake Montgomery . Produced by Anabel Bacon and Monica Espitia, engineered by Ivan Kuraev, executive producer Rachel Humphreys
description:
The tech industry spent big on the midterms, but it turned out to be a poor investment. Elon Musk poured a staggering $446m dollars into Republican-aligned political action committees (Pacs) and groups since last year, but his efforts didn’t pay off. Democrats won every one of the five Senate races where Musk’s America Pac spent the most money backing Republican candidates. Carter Sherman and Kai Wright are joined by the Guardian’s US tech editor, Blake Montgomery, to ask what the ‘blue tsunami’ will mean for Musk and the wider tech industry. Will this spell the end of AI datacenters? And if so, what could this mean for the US economy?

Continue reading.
title: Was Elon Musk the US midterms' biggest loser? – Stateside with Kai and Carter

author: Adrian Chiles
description:
Jude Bellingham’s new Calvin Klein ad campaign is heartening in so many ways, but the first thing I noticed was the capacious underpants

I have surprisingly strong feelings about underpants, or rather the celebrities who endorse them. I don’t have skin in the game; I’ve never been a designer-pants man. The nearest I got to any kind of endorsement deal was with the Björn Borg brand. They gave me some briefs, but, bafflingly, expressed no interest in photos of me wearing them. So I just wore them until they wore out, then went back to M&S.

While I cannot imagine ever buying Calvin Klein pants, I do take an interest in their models. I could have sworn blind David Beckham was one of them, but it turns out otherwise. Armani, H&M and Hugo Boss, but not Calvin Klein. Freddie Ljungberg was a CK man. Smouldering away, but a bit too much body oil for my taste. Looked a right slippery fish. The biggest letdown was
title: Big briefs for men are back – and I couldn’t be happier | Adrian Chiles

author: Anna Moore
description:
Daukes was an outgoing 10-year-old when he met boys’ club leader John Phillips. As an adult, he lived through years of chaos and self-sabotage, while repressing his experiences. Then he found out his brother had been abused by Phillips too

In early 2020, Johnny Daukes found an old storage box in his loft with a big black folder inside marked Toxic Hazard. It was stuffed with old sheets of paper: every song he’d written, starting as a teenager, just a boy with a guitar, then for Fin, his 90s indie band, and then his five solo albums.

By that time in his life, Daukes was 55 and deep in turmoil. He and his younger brother were working with the Metropolitan police to build a criminal case against the man who had sexually abused them both as children. Every case of historical abuse can disrupt a family, but this one was truly labyrinthine. Their abuser, John Phillips, had gone on to marry their sister and have 10 children. Every relationship was affected – cousins, siblings,
title: ‘By the time the abuse ended, I was 16, and a husk’: how Johnny Daukes survived his childhood – and fought back

author: Andy Beckett
description:
Two years in to her leadership, Badenoch continues to take the Tories ever-rightwards, into comfort-zone Conservatism

What happens to a political leader who is too sure of themself? Sometimes, huge confidence is a very useful, self-fulfilling quality: persuading party colleagues, activists, donors and voters that more can be achieved than is usually thought possible. Such utter conviction can keep everyone believing while the actual practicalities of a political project are worked out.

Yet when an air of absolute certainty turns out to be overconfidence, the bubble bursts. The politician may be revealed as disastrously complacent and lacking in judgment, having delusions of grandeur, or being fundamentally in denial. Especially in our era of online mockery and instinctive contempt for politicians, an overconfident leader can end up as a laughing stock.

Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist
title: No amount of sliding in the polls can shake Kemi Badenoch’s self-belief – or alter her party’s direction | Andy Beckett

author: Hannah Rochell
description:
The festive season isn’t known for its sustainability. This year, eschew throwaway decorations in favour of long-lasting, waste-free finds that you’ll use year after year

• The best homemade Christmas gift ideas

I met a woman one January who told me that every year she throws away her tree with all the decorations attached, and then just buys everything new the following year. Not only is this horrendous, environmentally speaking, but she’s missing out on the best bit, as far as I am concerned. For me, Christmas is all about nostalgia and sentimentality, and nothing speaks to that like taking the tatty little robin made of real feathers that belonged to my grandparents out of its storage box and nestling it into the branches of my tree.

My favourite day of the festive period isn’t actually Christmas Day, or even Christmas Eve. It’s
title: From recycled wreaths to fabric Advent calendars: 12 genuinely reusable Christmas things

author: Peter Bradshaw
description:
Apocryphal plans to send an arousing morale booster to troops battling the Nazis make scant sense, and nor does the resulting movie

Some potentially interesting ideas here and a good cast … but the whole thing disintegrates into a very weird and ill-judged mess. It looks as if it might be a saucy romp, but is in fact doomily serious, like a stilted, stricken stage play. Sexual violence, PTSD and misogyny are among the issues that the film fails to address convincingly.

Writer-director Richard Hawkins (who scripted Paul Greengrass’s The Theory of Flight) imagines that during the second world war the British government commissioned porn films to be shown to troops as a morale-boost. This is supposedly based on an “urban myth” whose existence does not appear to be evident other than in online material relating to this film – although Britain’s
title: Think of England review – far-fetched tale of state-sponsored second world war porn turns deadly serious

author: Graeme Wearden
description:
Rolling coverage of the latest economic and financial news, as UK braces for first interest rate rise in over three years

More succour for the Bank of England, and hard-pressed households!

Gas prices are dropping this morning, with the month-ahead UK gas price down 2% at 214.2p a therm.

Continue reading...
title: Bank of England expected to raise interest rates today; FTSE 100 hits three-month high – business live

author: Phil Harrison, Hannah J Davies and Priya Elan
description:
A riveting documentary following the rise of Marco Pierre White, Gordon Ramsay and Heston Blumenthal. Plus: the live final of Big Brother. Here’s what to watch this evening

9pm, BBC Two
“Gastronomy is the French Foreign Legion,” says Marco Pierre White. “They don’t question you too much.” In the 1980s, the culinary desert of the UK saw the rise of three difficult, brilliant chefs (Pierre White was joined by Gordon Ramsay and Heston Blumenthal) who triggered a foodie revolution. This three-parter doesn’t quite avoid presentational, era-specific cliches, but it does capture the energy generated by the trio’s rise. Phil Harrison

Continue reading...
title: TV tonight: how three rockstar chefs sparked a foodie revolution

author: Frances Ryan
description:
Despite the partial U-turn on care worker visas, the staff who keep the system afloat still face a hostile environment

If you want to see the senselessness of Britain’s immigration debate play out in real time, look no further than the crackdown on care workers’ visas that came to a head this week.

As part of its plans to force low-paid migrant workers to wait 15 years before settlement in the UK, the Home Office has been in a battle behind the scenes for the past six months to controversially include care workers in the policy. This is despite the social care system already facing critical staff shortages and the number of British citizens and immigrants taking the jobs dwindling.

Frances Ryan is a Guardian columnist
title: How irrational are Labour’s plans for migrant workers? To find out, read the small print

author: Jennifer Jones
description:
Liverpool: Their summer flowers provide the name and the fame, but this species is arguably at its best now

Beech mast crunches underfoot, and the occasional conker catches the sunlight, tiny beacons leading me to Camp Hill, south Liverpool, with its distant views over the Mersey estuary. Goldfinches erupt from desiccated knapweed, and a flock of pink-footed geese fly overhead. For once, the birds are not my goal, but a tree: the tulip tree (Liriodendron tulipifera).

Every autumn, the Camp Hill tulip tree flaunts its flamboyant presence: the Lady Gaga of the parkland. Named because its flowers resemble a tulip flower, and its leaves a tulip silhouette, few can resist its tulle lace canopy of butter-gold leaves. The luminescence is enhanced by the sheen of its leaf cuticles, and the fissured trunk adds yet more sensory impact. Yet this year there is a strangeness: instead of the golden monotone you would expect of this moment, there is a messy m
title: Country diary: The autumn glory of a tulip tree | Jennifer Jones

author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
description:
Amendment 81 would have required law enforcement to notify federal agents if people accused of violent crimes were not lawfully present in US

Colorado voters have spurned a conservative group’s effort to force police and prosecutors to aid the Trump administration’s mass deportation agenda.

Amendment 81, which failed to receive 55% of the vote on Tuesday, would have required Colorado’s law enforcement agents to notify federal immigration authorities if individuals accused of violent crime were not lawfully present in the US or if their legal status was undetermined.

Continue reading...
title: Colorado rejects conservative effort to require police to cooperate with immigration officers
